source.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
source.authors: Bo Gong; Shiyang Lai; James Evans; D. Song

page_placements.theme: Language-model neurons often carry several behaviours or lack a clean label

record.tranche_reason: The study examines polysemantic feature interference and neuron interventions, but does not test the claim's audit of human-interpretable neuron jobs or any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The study reports neuron-feature counts and effects of neuron manipulation, but does not test whether neuron poles have one or two human-namable jobs, explanation accuracy on held-out activations, or the other versioned claims. Those neuron-specific findings are recorded under fits_no_version. Other feature-steering and prompt-intervention results do not measure the claim's proposed interpretability audit.
record.test_reason: The study's neuron-level results count connections between neurons and clustered SAE features in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small. This is a related but different construct from the claim. It does not test whether neuron poles have one or two human-namable jobs, and it does not test explanations against held-out activations. It also does not address vision neurons, circuits built from neurons, or simulation-based explanation scores. Its main results concern interference-based steering and its transfer to larger models, which none of the versions name. These neuron findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only the secondary neuron result. The authors' main conclusion concerns interference between semantically unrelated but interfering SAE features. Steering with such features, via feature, token-gradient and prompt interventions, shifts next-token predictions toward a target. These interference patterns, found in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small, transfer to Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct. Fewer than 30% of the shared interference pairs have human-intelligible higher-order relations. The authors argue that polysemanticity is structured and not stochastic. Neuron sensitivity grows with polysemanticity, and super-neurons respond asymmetrically.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE feature clustering and feature, token-gradient, prompt, and neuron interventions; it does not use the pole-explanation audit or held-out explanation tests described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The neuron analysis uses feature clustering and a connection-strength threshold of 0.2; it focuses on strongly connected neurons and groups them by connected-feature count.

fits_no_version.finding: Among strongly connected neurons, more than 33% connect to only one or two aggregated SAE feature clusters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small, a substantial minority of strongly connected neurons link to one or two SAE feature clusters. This is not evidence of human-namable single jobs.

fits_no_version.finding: Polysemantic neurons strongly connected to aggregated features make up fewer than 5% of each layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under SAE-cluster connection thresholds, strongly connected polysemantic neurons are a small per-layer share in small LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Neurons with more connected features shift outputs more when masked or amplified. 'Super-neurons' (>500 features) show an asymmetry: amplification has large effects, masking small ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron intervention sensitivity scales with SAE-measured polysemanticity, with asymmetric effects for super-neurons.

record.problems: The study's neuron results concern SAE-cluster connections, not human-namable jobs or tested explanations. The reported neuron-intervention plots do not have numerical values in the text. The authors note that SAE features can vary with dimensionality and hyperparameters, and that neuron interventions focus on one feature in one layer.
record.rows_left_out: Other feature-direction, token-gradient, prompt-injection, and HellaSwag intervention outcomes were not included because they do not measure neuron interpretability or the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: The Qwen3-32B pole audit shares (about 90% one job, 7% two related jobs, 2–4% not understood).
Shares of interpretable neuron poles across dense and mixture-of-experts models and scale. Only small-model SAE-cluster counts are reported.
InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, pose explanation, recursive generalization.
Effects of architecture, regularization or tools on the share of interpretable neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without replacement models.
Whether explanations that fit activating examples predict held-out firing.

record.verdict_notes: R1 and R2 use different denominators: strongly connected neurons versus all neurons per layer. Neither should be read as a share of interpretable neurons. The post-hoc annotation (27.7% of interfering pairs show a plausible association) concerns SAE feature pairs, not neurons. It does not bear on any version. Operation types for R3–R6 should be activation scaling rather than weight edits.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit shares, job descriptions, and held-out activation tests.
Cross-model and scale comparisons of the claimed shares of interpretable neuron poles, including dense and mixture-of-experts models up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car examples, pose explanations, and recursive generalization.
Effects of architecture, regularization, or tools on the share of interpretable neurons, including the vision-model estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from model neurons explain behavior without replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitting activating examples fail to predict held-out firing.
Automated explanation scores based on simulated activations on new text.
